subtopic: TRIBUTE TO MADAM DENYSE BELANGER-ROCHON OF MONTPELLIER, P.Q.
TRIBUTE TO MADAM DENYSE BELANGER-ROCHON OF MONTPELLIER, P.Q.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today, the Persons Awards prize will be awarded to five Canadian women for their contribution to the advancement of the status of women in Canada. The House will recall that on October 18, 1929, the right of Canadian women to sit in the Senate was recognized, following a petition to give women the status of persons in the British North America Act.
This day is a very special one for my own riding in Argenteuil-Papineau, since one of the prize winners, Mrs. Denyse Belanger-Rochon, comes from Montpellier, and she will be receiving her award shortly from the Governor General of Canada. Mrs. Rochon, former president of the Quebec Federation of Women, has pressured the federal Government and the Government of Quebec to improve their record on such important issues as employment equity, impact of technological change on working women, pensions, daycare,
and the like. Mrs. Rochon deserves our admiration, and we want to extend to her our sincere congratulations for her work in general and her contribution toward advancing the cause of Canadian women, and we also wish to congratulate the other prize winners.

Mr. Speaker, the Conservative Government has defended its decision to build a maximum security institution in the Prime Minister's (Mr. Mulroney) riding as an exercise in job creation. Phoney statistics have been cited to support the decision, but whether Manicouagan has higher unemployment than any other Quebec riding is not the point. Job-creation projects should be job-creation projects, placed where most needed to provide good, productive jobs. If the Government wants to justify a particular project it must demonstrate how many jobs will be created at what cost, and that its proposed measure would be more effective than other measures for job creation. The Government has not done this.
Prison construction should never be used as job creation anyway, and the fact that the Liberals were just as bad is no excuse. Decisions about prison placement should be made according to correctional principles and, on this, opinion is unanimous. Port-Cartier is totally inappropriate, as was Renous which was built by the Liberals according to the same reprehensible, opportunistic, and misguided motives as Port-Cartier.

subsubtopic: CRITICISM OF GOVERNMENT POLICIES AFFECTING UNEMPLOYED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to express my shock and dismay at the concerted attack of the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) and his Department on the unemployed of the country.
First, unemployed Canadians were hit with a $100 million cut in job-creation funds. Second, there were changes to unemployment insurance which negatively affected members of the Canadian Armed Forces and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. Third, the Forget Commission has called on the Government to reduce assistance further to Canada's unemployed. Fourth, the Minister has said that there will be no short-term job-creation programs this year, programs which would have provided desperately needed assistance to many Canadians. Fifth, the Minister is now cutting back on the staff in his Department, staff which is badly needed to assist Canada's unemployed in finding work.
Canadians want a Government which does not attack the weakest and least fortunate segments of our society. They want a Government which is caring and is concerned about the unemployed and will provide long-term meaningful jobs to the thousands of Canadians across the country who desperately need employment.

speakeroldname: Mr. Lawrence I. O'Neil (Cape Breton Highlands-Canso):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to challenge the attitude of opposition Members who feel that regional development should not be a
government priority. Their view is that if it costs more to do it in the regions of the country it should not be done.
As a Member from one of Canada's disadvantaged regions, I want to tell those critics that Canadians living in the regions strongly support the commitment of the Government of Canada to solving the problem of regional economic disparity. Incurring greater capital costs or operating expenses for the purpose of enhancing economic opportunities in the regions is surely far more constructive an approach than that which calls for continuation of social assistance and UIC payments, with no hope of employment for these needy Canadians. Those payments also amount to millions of dollars each year.
Regrettably, the Liberals and the NDP appear opposed to initiatives which will mean improved economic circumstances for Canadians living in the regions.

subsubtopic: CALL FOR NEW PROGRAMS TO ASSIST POOR
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the National Council of Welfare reported that almost four million Canadians are presently living in poverty. Many of them are youngsters under 16 years of age. It is a disgrace that this situation exists in a country as wealthy as Canada. It is obvious that the system of welfare which was developed has broken down and no longer meets the needs of people whose needs are so great. I call upon the Government of Canada to work with the provinces, rethink the programs we have established, and to establish new programs which will meet the needs of our poor.

During the summer recess, Mr. Speaker, I took it upon myself to travel throughout my riding of East Quebec and call on most businessmen who had availed themselves of the Challenge 86 summer employment program. In Quebec East, Mr. Speaker, 82 businesses and community organizations joined this program under which 221 jobs were created and $327,158 invested in the future of our young people. All employers with whom I met were enthusiastic about the work done by students and stated that this Government program has been a great help to them.
October 22, 1986

As to the students themselves, they candidly admit that without this program they would have been hard pressed to find such remunerative employment related to their studies or prospective career. I was even able to ascertain that some of them changed their career plans after this experience because they came to the conclusion that the work they were asked to perform was not really what they had expected in the first place. Mr. Speaker, I can only echo the feelings expressed by many of them and hope that the Challenge program will continue for years to come.

According to the Auditor General's report, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of National Revenue has granted tax credits valued at $225 million more than the Post Canada deficit. Yet a few days ago, Mr. Speaker, we learned that Canada Post intends to boost first-class postage by 2 cents and slap charges on people who do not benefit from home delivery and others who receive special delivery items. In light of the Auditor General's report, Mr. Speaker, I should think that the Minister responsible for Canada Post ought to instruct Canada Post officials to stop forthwith any procedure aimed at increasing the cost of services to Canadians, and to restore full delivery service throughout the country.

subsubtopic: INABILITY TO ACCOUNT FOR EXPENDITURE OF PUBLIC FUNDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canadians are deeply concerned about the Auditor General's reporting the unaccountability of $57 million by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. Not only is this an unaccountability of CBC funds, but it is most importantly an unaccountability of Canadian taxpayers' money.
In a time of deficit reduction and curtailed spending this lack of accountancy organization exhibited by the CBC must be investigated. Parliament must be concerned with the lack of business organization demonstrated by the Corporation. I urge that a complete study of the Auditor General's reported inability to pass audit be commenced as soon as possible. Parliament must make every effort to make the CBC accountable and responsible.

subsubtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA FISHERMEN-INABILITY TO VOTE IN PROVINCIAL ELECTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
2,000	B.C. fishermen will be effectively disenfranchised from voting in today's B.C. election, because no arrangements were made by the Department of Fisheries and Oceans and the B.C. Elections Branch. The Department announced a fisheries opening in the Johnstone Strait on Monday. That meant fishermen from Vancouver to northern Vancouver Island had to leave their homes early this morning; therefore they cannot vote in today's provincial election. They did not have the opportunity to vote in the advance poll, because the opening was not announced until Monday, and the advance poll closed last week.
It is disturbing that the Department of Fisheries and Oceans and the B.C. Elections Branch were not able to arrange for voting to take place on the fishing grounds, or for earlier notice. As it is, the Elections Branch is saying that no facilities could be provided. Democracy is more important than this kind of buck passing.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to express today in this House my deepest feeling of dissatisfaction concerning the current leaks about the Forget report scheduled to be tabled in late November. Over a year ago now, Mr. Speaker, our Government set up an inquiry commission to examine thoroughly the whole unemployment insurance scheme and the related legislation which goes back over 45 years. We asked the Forget Commission to submit a report, so that we might amend and improve the unemployment insurance scheme. Mr. Speaker, six qualified people have been mandated to report to the Government at a cost of some $5.6 million to Canadian taxpayers.
Mr. Speaker, I acknowledge that members of a commission may disagree with the content of a report, but it is altogether a different story when leaking information results in creating confusion among the public, and this, even before the final report is tabled. The situation is such that one wonders what has happened to professional ethic.

October 22, 1986

Mr. Speaker, I want to share with the House a letter which was sent to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) by one of my constituents, Mr. David Villeneuve of Navan, Ontario. It reads:
I write in regard to the planned cuts at NRC.
An important and widely supported part of the Conservative election platform was to increase Canadian R&D to world levels, yet we have seen nothing but budget cuts and layoffs.
NRC has been hit three times, in November, 1984, in the government-wide cuts of November, 1985, and now the space station cuts. Surely that is enough.
All industrialized nations have national laboratories of some sort; ours is NRC. I urge the Prime Minister to listen to my constituent, Mr. Villeneuve.

speakerposition: Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to begin by thanking the Hon. Member for providing the House with a rare opportunity to discuss what I consider to be the most important and critical issue that will face us as a society in the next 10 to 15 years. What we do collectively as a people in the field of science and technology over the next 10 to 15 years will certainly determine the role we will play in the next century among the community of nations.
It is within our grasp to position ourselves to be among the leaders in the world. It is within our grasp to respond to the challenges that are thrust upon us at such a relentless pace, brought about by this new technological revolution, and to respond to them in a positive, enthusiastic and confident fashion. As well, it is perhaps possible to be pushed out of the fast current that takes humankind into a new age, to be resigned to the backwaters of mediocrity, to be resigned to obscurity and insignificance.
This place never ceases to amaze me. It is interesting to hear how many different aspects of the truth some Hon. Members manage to put on the record. They defend their aspects of the truth with such conviction, sometimes even against their better judgment. If the Hon. Member who just spoke were in a courtroom, there would be no doubt in my mind at all that someone would charge him with perjury.
This debate is most timely because Hon. Members have, during the last two or three weeks, put so many different aspects of the truth on the record that it is extremely urgent for me to familiarize the House with some of the real facts today. Perhaps I should begin by setting the record straight regarding the aspersions that were cast in connection with the NRC.
There is no doubt that the National Research Council has been, is and will remain Canada's principal research establishment. However, the institute must continue as it has in the past to stay in tune with the times, to respond quickly and very effectively to new situations and new realities. One of these new realities is that much more research of the basic kind is today being performed in the private sector, and much more than ever before, research is being performed in universities. That shift has not occurred as a result of any deliberate policy of any Government. The reason for that shift is that it is becoming ever more critical that fundamental research be combined with the training of a future generation of scientists. That teaching happens to be best performed in universities.
In the period before World War II, there were 51 universities of which 19 were doing research that qualified for grants that the National Research Council gave to universities for research and training. In 1986, there are 82 universities in Canada of which 50 are receiving NSERC grants for the purpose of research and the training of future scientists. It is because of that that we have put an emphasis on university

October 22, 1986

funding. The statement made by the Member that there is not a significant increase in university funding is literally untrue.
We have put in place a program which will deliver, over a five-year period, $1 billion of additional new money for university research and the training of future scientists. I make no apologies at all for the fact that some of this funding is tied to a matching formula which requires the private sector to respond. As a result, 50 cents of private sector investment will trigger a $2 world class research effort in our universities. That is not a bad record at all.
We need to boost our international competitiveness and we need to forge important linkages between the science community, our in-house government laboratories and the private sector. The deficit gap which is much too wide was created by a former Government. This gap must be closed.
However, let us look for a moment at these so-called cuts the Hon. Member said have occurred to the NRC over the last three or four years. The NRC breaks down its budgetary calculations into three different categories. The first category is the operating budget, the budget that pays for research, for management and for the operation of those things under the Council's responsibility. Then there is the so-called transfer budget. That is used to finance extramural laboratories such as TRIUMF in British Columbia and other outside research laboratories which are operating at arm's length but are partners with the Research Council.
This budget includes the IRAP program which the Hon. Member, over the last three weeks, consistently proclaimed had been drastically cut. Has he had the grace to apologize and to say that there were no cuts to the IRAP program? No. Again, perjury would be the charge in a courtroom.
Finally, there is the capital budget. This is the budget that the NRC uses to build buildings, to buy equipment and to do things which are normally done. It is in the capital budget where some of the cuts have occurred and I will tell the House why that is.
Unlike the former Government, we do not believe that the cause of science and technology is dramatically advanced by bricks and mortar, by building edifices, palaces and monuments all over the country. However, the former Government did believe that. It thought that the way to increase the government effort was to build buildings all over the place. There are three such buildings which the Hon. Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Siddon) had mentioned. There is the Ocean Dynamics Laboratory in Newfoundland, the Biotechnology Centre in Montreal and the Industrial Technology Centre in Winnipeg. The cost of these three structures is $157 million. These buildings were built over the last four years; and a couple of them are already in operation and the other one will be commissioned in February. Obviously the budget of the NRC had to be increased by $157 million to pay for these buildings. Obviously, as these buildings are completed and are being commissioned, the budget of the NRC decreases in accordance with the completion of these buildings.
Let me just tell the House what actually happened to the budget of the NRC.
Incidentally, the NRC budget was never at $520 million. Again, the Hon. Member has a selective memory. When he mentioned the peak figure of the NRC's budget, he conveniently added the supplementary income the NRC receives aside from government funding, income earned through charges for services and so on. In 1984-85, this income amounted to $40 million. The budget of the NRC in that year, the peak year, was not $520 million but $480 million. Then when the Hon. Member mentioned the low figure, this year's figure, he conveniently said that the budget is now $398 million, but he did not add the extra income. These are the kinds of dishonest games these people play when they make their points.
The fact is that the operating budget of the NRC has stayed consistent and level. I have a chart here. Perhaps the Hon. Member cannot read very well. I will send it over to him. It is a picture. Perhaps the Hon. Member could get a better assessment of it.
The operations budget of the NRC, which is the highest component, stays reasonably level. There has been no decrease. The transfer budget, of which I spoke, again is the green line. It stays level. There has been no decrease. When I look at the equipment and the building budget, of course, there is a sharp incline into 1984-85, and then a decrease as the construction programs were completed.
Please, Mr. Speaker, through you to the Hon. Member, let us have a little more honesty and integrity when one speaks about these important things. It has not been very helpful to the management of the NRC to maintain any kind of morale with this kind of gamesmanship. Incidentally, the Hon. Member is no stranger to the truth. He has been invited consistently to attend briefing meetings. He knows the truth. He plays games in the House of Commons. While he may have had a weekend headline and while he may have even succeeded in embarrassing the Government slightly with his stretching of the truth, he has destroyed to a great extent and has been personally responsible to a great extent for the destruction of the morale at the National Research Council, which has always been very high and which has now been severely damaged.
Hear, hear!

Member said that there was a consistent increase in the over-all spending in terms of the Gross National Product. If you destroy the economy and the Gross National Product declines, you have a consistent increase in percentages in your R and D expenditures, and that is what happened.

The previous administration was also looking for a modern industrial image for our country, an image which identified our traditional industries like agriculture, mining, forestry and fishing as unsophisticated rural occupations, something from which a nation in search of a modern industrial image must get away. Give that to the developing countries. Let us shape our image after perhaps Japan and Germany. Those were the models that were held out as a nation seeking a modern industrial image. That is what we were to emulate.
All we had to do to achieve that image was to spend as much in terms of the Gross National Product as Germany and Japan does, and everything would fall into place. It is true that we cannot fault the former Government for the sense of urgency that it brought to the mission. Money was absolutely no object. It was doing roughly half of what it normally should in research and development. To prove our inhouse situation-about which I have already spoken-all we had to do was build modern world-class buildings, which we have. My compliments to the architects. But nobody thought of designing any programs to fit into these buildings. They called them world-class buildings and it is now my job to provide the programs. That is all that had to be done to improve the internal performance.
The former Government knew that action was required because we were chalking up a deficit in high-tech trade with other countries that was growing at a rate of 15 per cent a cent a year and had reached $10 billion a year by 1984. What did the former Liberal Government do, Mr. Speaker? It acted swiftly and with conviction to bring in the so-called scientific research tax credit. That was to stimulate private sector activity quickly. Indeed, it did. Did it ever stimulate private sector activity. There was a lot of activity in innovative tax accounting, but there was no innovative technology created.

will have to cut the deficit. He said we have to double our effort. That was the goal and it was duly incorporated into the campaign material of the Conservative Party in 1984 in the form of a 2.5 per cent target for R and D.
What has happened since then? Do we have a goal of 2.5 per cent or even 2.2 per cent or 1.8 per cent, to give the Prime Minister every possible benefit of the doubt in setting a target? No, we have a spending level of about 1.3 per cent, or an amount, to again use the Prime Minister's words, which will ensure that Canada will, "during its entire lifetime play in the junior B circuit".
Junior B Government.

My colleague gives the Government too high a grade.
Then we have the Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Oberle) saying during the Throne Speech debate, in answer to me, that he "chose to ask the science council to help me establish realistic funding targets by examining each sector of our industry and by comparing what they are doing with what their competitors are doing in other parts of the world. We will establish realistic targets." More bafflegab and of course more delay. The reason we have not doubled our R and D expenditure to meet the Prime Minister's most insistent demand is that we must now find, to use the Minister's words, "realistic targets". In other words, we have to reduce the deficit and that is more important and comes before everything else.
The Prime Minister also insisted in 1983 that research and development must not be sacrificed to financial restraint. He knew then that there is no point in eating the seed corn which will produce a larger and more bountiful harvest ahead. He has forgotten about that. We are now back to cutting the deficit before we can invest in scientific research and development. He criticized the Liberals for applying the six and five restraints to public R and D. On page 40 of his book he said "The National Research Council, which acts as Canada's main research laboratory, needs a funding increase of at least 20 per cent to bring it up to $400 million." That was in 1983. On Friday we had the president of the NRC reported in The Ottawa Citizen as saying that his budget four years later was just $400 million, having been $520 million the year before.
As we know, the NRC is now wrestling with the tragic loss of programs, research teams, low staff morale and administrative chaos, all of which were caused by the further $20 million cut announced last week after the cuts made last year. I will return to that, and particularly to the inept and deceiving performance of the Minister throughout this most grevious of injuries to one of our most useful research institutions.
Let us now return to the Prime Minister. In his book he was so certain that he had found the way ahead for Canada that he described the chairman of the NRC as a "public servant who understands the problems of the real world and the frustrations that go with it". He quoted him as follows:
If Canada implements something like this plan it will still have problems in the years ahead, but these will be the problems of excellence, the worries of the rich. They will probably include a scarcity of workers rather than unemployment, a surplus of affordable energy, much of it renewable, and so low a national debt that we may be pressured as Japan is now to limit our exports.
What was the plan that was to increase our national wealth and provide this passport to easy street from mean street? It was a long-range plan for research and development in Canada which has been rejected and, further, systematically undermined by the Government since it took office. If the Prime Minister, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), the successive Ministers of Science and Technology and the entire Cabinet wish to know why we have not attained the R and D target and the problems of wealth which go with it, they need only look in the mirror. Research has been a target for cuts by the Government rather than a national goal. Line departments, granting councils and research organizations such as the NRC have all been cut back.
Throughout these cuts from public bodies we have heard the Government's refrain that private sector research will increase and fill the gaps. We have some pretty realistic evidence on this today in this week's Financial Post which has a special section on R and D in the private sector. They say, "Industrial R and D spending slows, researchers will be on a stricter diet". They go on to analyse what was reported to them by the private sector and forecast a 3 per cent increase in R and D from sample companies compared to a 14 per cent increase last year. Only 9 of 80 of the largest R and D firms in the country said they were planning substantial increases in R and D budgets over the next three years.
The Government's rhetoric insists that private R and D play an increasing role in our entire research effort. That is a laudible goal, especially since only 3 per cent of Canadian companies of any size do any research, but it is not happening. In particular, it is not happening on anywhere near the scale the Prime Minister indicated it would when he wrote his book and the Conservatives were campaigning for office in 1984. That is probably not happening because so many of our largest companies are multinational corporations which prefer to do their R and D at home base rather than in Canada.
Just to emphasize that point, I want to compare our R and D figure of 1.3 per cent Gross National Product, which has not varied much under Liberal and Conservative Governments since 1983, with the 2.7 per cent invested in the United States, 2.61 per cent in Japan, 2.58 per cent in Germany, and 2.47 per cent in Sweden, a country much smaller in population than Canada. All these countries have research efforts of close to 100 per cent higher than Canada.
We are a Junior B team.

As my colleague points out, we are a Junior B team which the Prime Minister deplored when he was in Opposition.
October 22, 1986

In making this contrast I will relate it to what is happening to those persons who are charged with carrying out research in Canada. For them this R and D percentage is no abstract figure. It represents laboratories, equipment, research personnel and support and grants to carry out research and find its application. Those are lacking in Canada to a large extent because of the lack of adequate funding.
Canada has been fortunate in the awarding of the Nobel prize for distinguished achievement in chemistry to Dr. John Polanyi. Dr. Polanyi has brought considerable honour to Canada for his achievement and he has been extremely gracious in thanking this country for providing the means by which his discoveries in chemistry were made.
In one article Dr. Polanyi paid tribute to the NRC, the place where he began his post-doctoral research. He said it exuded "-an amazing spirit of liberality. It endeared the NRC and Canada to me. The spirit of co-operation was splendid. It was a great place to do science". You will note the past tense, Mr. Speaker. It is very important.
In another more recent interview Dr. Polanyi was asked this question: "Do you think if you were a graduate student today and in similar situations to the time when you actually were a graduate student that you would come to Canada? Do you think there's the same kind of opportunities for scientists in Canada today"? In response Dr. Polanyi said: "Well, honestly, no I don't think so. I think I would go to the U.S. And I think we have it in us not only to compete in every other way of comparable quality and excitement here. But we haven't chosen to do so".
Compare those observations by the Nobel prize winner, Dr. Polanyi, with the nonsense we hear from the Minister of Stae for Science and Technology. Out of such thoughtful assessment by persons who know is the brain-drain born and accelerated. Dr. Polanyi has not lost hope for Canada. Indeed, he wonders why we have not done better. He put it this way: "In a country where the rhetoric about science is so splendid, you know it's getting better all the time. In fact what is done is not really remotely commensurate". He went on to question why Canadians are not more science-minded and he hopes that we will develop "the taste and pride in that endeavour". He then adds the clincher: "Because it's important to us, not just as a nation, which is of course absolutely vital, but in addition it's very important to us, as everybody keeps saying in their marvelous speeches, as a base on which to rest the technology that we have to have".
It sounds as if he has been listening to the Prime Minister and the Minister of State for Science and Technology, but they don't seem to be listening to Dr. Polanyi. He means what he says but they just talk about it. They worry more about the deficit than they do about research and development.
According to the Minister, Dr. Polanyi did his work at the University of Toronto, not at the NRC. Therefore, I assume that according to the Minister we should not pay too much attention to what Dr. Polanyi says. All this conveniently

forgets that if the NRC had not offered him a position when he was preparing to move from Great Britain he would have gone elsewhere rather than to Canada. People that good are never short of offers.
We can conclude from all this what might happen to the future of other scientists like Dr. Polanyi. They are being told by the Government that there is no place for them in Canada. Dr. Polanyi's lab at the NRC is being shut down. The NRC is being systematically gutted through funding cuts. No wonder distinguished professors are reluctantly concluding that their brightest students will do better by going elsewhere.
Perhaps the Government opposite believes that it is fooling Canadians with its talk of increased funding for research, but it really is not. Those who analyze the policies and those who have to live with the end results know that the dollars are not there. The companies surveyed by the Financial Post certainly know what is really happening. They know that the spending cap placed on transfers to the provinces for federal contributions to post-secondary education means hundreds of millions of dollars less to the year 1991. They know that the so-called billion dollars for the three granting councils of the federal Government, the NSERC, the SSHRC, and the MRC really means that their base funding has been frozen until 1991 and that any increase is entirely contingent on contributions from the private sector. They know that the so-called billion dollars for university research is not a billion dollars at all, but more like $300 million and will be only encouraging research which the private sector wants rather than what we really need.
They know that government research is in fact contracting. The NRC is on the ropes, its purposes distorted for the public relations gesture which the Government wants in space. Its own research, which has already been examined and approved by international panels, is simply ignored by the Government and shunted aside.
They know that line departments with significant research capabilities including agriculture, fisheries, the environment, forestry and mining, where most of the people who have jobs in the country are working and where most people will work in the next generation, have been substantially cut back. They know that Canada's is probably the only government in the western world with a forestry ministry which has no forestry research capability because the former Conservative Government, headed by the present Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) sold the forestry labs. They know all this and they discount what the Government opposite is saying. Many persons who are knowledgeable in the science policy field are now speaking out about the shortcomings of this Government's policy. Gordon MacNabb, the retired President of NSERC said this about the failure of the Government to fund adequately a five-year research program:
My greatest frustration was having worked so long and hard on the logic of the plan. I don't mind losing a battle, but I've never had a chance to fight. No one really argued against our manpower projections, and what we said about the shortage of talented people we're going to have.

Surely that shows that this Government's mind is made up. It does not want to know about research, particularly about basic research, which the Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Oberle) quaintly and mistakenly calls "curiosity research". It does not want anyone with ideas that may differ from its own. This is clearly a recipe for disaster. One aspect of that disaster is being played out this week with the Minister of State insisting that there were "no cuts" and "no programs lost" at the NRC as the evidence came out that whole divisions and programs were being wound up and there were more than 100 persons who could not be fitted into the various retraining and early retirement schemes. No wonder this Government has another credibility problem to add to all the others. It is regrettable, to say the least, that their statements about research and development do not match their actions. But it is far more serious than that. Progress is nowhere at the level that everyone recommends, including the Government. The research community is progressively more disheartened. Canada, a supposedly young country open to new ideas, is in reality lagging behind in every vital research area.
The conclusion is inescapable and despite the efforts of the Government to say the opposite, the reality is increasingly obvious to anyone who cares to look.
Hear, hear!

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Laurier (Mr. Berger) earlier made reference to the new funding formula for universities as a formula that would have the result of freezing the university research funding budget. The program is designed not to be a ceiling but to be a floor and to give a clear indication to the universities what they will have in their A-base-unlike the way it used to be before, as the Hon. Member will recall-where there were certain amounts of money put into the Main Estimates and in September there would be a Supplementary Estimate and perhaps another one in February. When I assumed the portfolio, my first task was to add another $16 million to university research in the last year. I do not know what kind of planning had gone into spending that money from February until the end of March. There were three principles: Number one was to stabilize the funding and put the money in the A-base up front, so there could be forward and intelligent planning. Number two was to increase university funding significantly, which we did. Number three was to forge these industrial linkages.
1 know that the Hon. Member is sincere in not being informed. But I would like him to know that there is nothing to stop the Minister or the Government from coming forward in March or the fall of any year and identifying new priorities and adding additional funding to the A-base. That has always been the case. This was not a freeze, but merely an attempt to stabilize university funding, which everyone recognized as a major priority.

It is not me or other Members of Parliament that the Hon. Minister has to convince that research funding at the universities has not and will not be cut further. It is the universities. I asked the Minister to stop reading his own press releases and to read the submissions made by the Association of Canadian Universities and Colleges and the Canadian Association of University Teachers. They document clearly the fact that cuts have been made and are being made by this Government, not just to research and development work at the university, but to all university funding. The reductions in the established finance programs automatically mean reductions for the universities. So much of what the Minister and the Government have promised in the way of increases for research and development depends upon increases in funding by the private sector.
The Minister and I do not agree on many things, but I am sure he will agree with me that The Financial Post is not some wild-eyed, woolly, socialist, impractical rag. The current issue of The Financial Post contains a special report regarding research and development with a headline reading "Industrial R & D spending slows". The sub-heading is "Researchers will be on a stricter diet". I would like to quote the following couple of sentences:
After substantial increases in Research and Development budgets in 1985, Canadian companies will barely boost their spending this year. The Financial Post's exclusive annual survey shows total expenditure on industrial R & D is expected to rise by a little more than 3 per cent-
The 76 private-sector firms that provided complete figures have allocated $1.43 billion to R & D in Canada this year, up 3.5 per cent from 1985's, $1.39 billion.
The 10 Crown agencies providing complete data proposed to spend $327 million in Canada, up 2 per cent from 1985.
There are the facts as given to The Financial Post by the major companies that do research. They are talking about increases of 2 and 3 per cent on their research which was inadequate until now. Where is the tremendous increase in the private sector research on which the whole plan of the Minister and the Government is based, which is absolutely necessary and which is a corner-stone of the so-called plan and strategy of the Government? It is not there. The whole thing will collapse like a house of cards in the very near future.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) attended the press conference given by Dr. Kerwin last week. He heard what Dr. Kerwin had to say about lay-offs at the National Research Council. Dr. Kerwin said that in the past two years the NRC has had to deal with the loss of 400 positions. It used all the tools at its disposal to avoid lay-offs. It imposed a hiring freeze, did not fill vacancies, used early retirements, shifts within the National Research Council, and it was able to minimize the number of lay-offs so there were very few lay-offs. As I recall, he said that with the 200 positions that the Council will lose as a result of this government cut imposed last week, it will be difficult to avoid lay-offs because the fat has been cut out.
In the light of what Dr. Kerwin said last week, what does the Hon. Member have to say about the Minister's argument?

The Minister first said in this Elouse: "There will be no layoffs at the NRC". That was unequivocal. He now has said that there will be no lay-offs at the NRC this year. Then he has gone on to say that he will do everything in his power to place these people in the private sector or in universities. The question to the Hon. Member is: When people have to leave the NRC as a result of this budget cut but find employment at universities or in the private sector, does this constitute a layoff in his mind, or the mind of the average Canadian?

Mr. Speaker, as a loyal and competent senior public servant, Dr. Kerwin was very careful, walking on eggshells, in order not to have to criticize the Government publicly. However, if one had listened to Dr. Kerwin and if one had read The Ottawa Citizen since Dr. Kerwin had his press conference, one would know of actual cases such as that of the physicist with a world famous reputation who, at age 62, is taking early retirement because the Government said to him: "We will sweeten your retirement fund if you retire now so we will have a vacancy for a younger scientist whom we will not have to lay off'. There is a similar story with respect to a senior chemist. There are dozens of stories like that. In no way can the NRC not make substantial reductions in its staff if it has to accept the budget which is being forced on it.
I hope the Chairman of the standing committee which is meeting tonight will agree that the committee should in the very near future invite senior officals of the NRC, and probably senior officials of the other granting councils, to come before committee and let them say what is really happening and what will happen. Let them answer with facts the kind of nonsense we have heard again and again from the Minister.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to have this opportunity to speak to the Opposition motion condemning the Government's present policy on research and development, and I am taking part in this debate because something very important is at stake.
First of all, this is a matter of particular concern to me. For many years I have taken an active part in the work of the committee that examines the appropriations for various federal agencies involved in research and development. I am equally concerned about the Government's policy or desire to cut back on research in our universities, because in my riding, Mr. Speaker, in Ottawa-Vanier, we have the University of Ottawa, a university that is internationally known for the quality of its research. I am therefore distressed about the lack of concern for this very important issue. Mr. Speaker, I need hardly recall that the riding of Ottawa-Vanier also includes the headquarters of the National Research Council's Science and Engineering Centre.
I say this because this particular building is in my riding, there are many people who work there, and from the telephone calls I have been receiving in the past two or three days, these people are concerned, and they have good reason to be concerned, because their future, the future of this country and the future of our young people is at stake.
I say this with considerable emphasis because I have also received phone calls from university students and professors which were often about the need for increasing research and development in this country. Last Sunday, Mr. Speaker, I was attending a convocation ceremony at the University of Ottawa. It was held Sunday morning-one of my sons was receiving his diploma-and I was very, very impressed by the calibre of the students who were receiving their Master's degrees and Ph.D.s.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, the people of my riding have a direct interest in research and development; I am personally interested because it affects at least 13,000 university students, because it affects the residents of my riding who work in this field, and as I said earlier because it also affects the science and engineering research centre about which my constituents are concerned since it has to do with their career.
Mr. Speaker, the Government's approach to this issue is deplorable and, unfortunately, we will have to live with the consequences for years to come. I am not unduly alarmed, far from it, but all one need do is read the press comments of the last few days to see to what extent public opinion is concerned about this issue. Indeed the Prime Minister himself said so in his many statements, and perhaps I might repeat the words of the Hon. Member for Laurier (Mr. Berger) who quoted straight from the Prime Minister's book, the Prime Minister's political credo. I quote:

"The National Research Council which acts as Canada's main research laboratory needs a funding increase of at least 20 per cent to bring it up to approximately $400 million".

Mr. Speaker, he said that in 1983, and we are now in 1986; if the level had been maintained in constant dollars, there would clearly have been a reduction, which would have been unfortunate. In his election platform, the Prime Minister had promised to double the funds available for research and development. What is he doing today? Exactly the opposite. He is slashing the budget of the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada by forcing it to cut over $20 million, which could result in over 200 positions being lost, and he is reducing nearly by half, to only 1.3 per cent, his stated goal of increasing the funds available to 2.5 per cent of the Gross National Product. In a way, we are getting used to seeing this Government cutting staffs, budgets, and funds available for research. It makes you wonder, the way this Government behaves; it is truly conservative and not very progressive.
We are now told about $20 million being cut and 200 jobs being lost. But Hon. Members should not forget that since the Progressive Conservative Party came to power, it is $120 million which have been cut and over 600 jobs which have been lost at the National Research Council alone.
The situation of research in universities is not any better. They are also severely affected by budget cuts. For instance, the authorities at Ottawa U. this year have seriously considered the possibility of eliminating research funds completely. Fortunately, they have managed to avoid making such a deplorable decision, but what will happen next year? When we know that 17,000 Canadians are getting funds from the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada, and that most Canadian universities are dependent on it for their necessary equipment, equipment they cannot do without, this is indeed disturbing. What does the Conservative Government want to do with our universities, if it cuts off their resources? Mr. Speaker, a university is not a secondary school. It is a centre for research. Canada's economic development depends on our ability to train competent researchers, engineers and technicians.
Mr. Speaker, as we all know, our economy depends largely on our exports. In fact, among the OECD countries, only the Federal Republic of Germany ranks higher than Canada in its dependence on exports. Expressed in terms of a percentage of the Gross National Product, exports account for 30 per cent of the GNP in Germany and 28 per cent in our country.
In fact, yesterday the federal Minister of Labour (Mr. Cadieux) said, I believe, at a press conference at the Development Centre of the Montreal School of Business Administration: "We must not forget that a loss of only 10 per cent of the jobs connected with our exports to the United States may mean that 250,000 Canadian jobs will disappear."
Mr. Speaker, if we look at how the present Government is behaving, we get the impression it is not conscious of these facts. They talk but they do not act. However, when the Minister compared Canada's rate of investment in research

and development with that of our trading partners, the Prime Minister himself stated:
The governments of these other countries have understood-that the jobs of tomorrow, the pursuit of their high standard of living, the health of their economy, depend on the success or failure of their technologies.

And what does he do now, Mr. Speaker, now that he is in power? He introduces legislation, introduces Government measures that will sabotage the progress of technology and science in this country. In yesterday's Toronto Star, Mr. Speaker, we find an article in which the Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Oberle) is reported as saying, and I quote the Toronto Star:

The minister, who has repeatedly said publicly that Canada is nearing a crisis because of its $12.5 billion trade deficit in high-tech products, said Canada is on its way to becoming a "banana republic by the year 2000" if it does not start adapting technology much more quickly in its traditional industries.

However, Mr. Speaker, we should not be suprised by what the Conservative Government is doing about research. The Conservatives acted in a similar manner in the famous case of the Arrow, a scientific research and development program of the aeronautical industry which was abandoned and destroyed by a Conservative Government.
The Conservatives were also saying at the time that this program was too costly and that it was the result of an irresponsible decision. The exodus of these researchers, engineers and highly specialized workers ... I was told this morning that it takes from 10 to 15 years to train one scientist with world-recognized qualifications and that it is very difficult to replace these people when there is no more work for them and they are forced to move to other countries.

National Research Council. This person called me to say how irritated and angry he was at the reluctance of this Government to provide financial support for research. He gave me a list of names which I could repeat to the Hon. Member, but it would not serve much purpose.

As I see it, this Government is about to make the same mistake as was made in the case of the Arrow, the unfortunate decision to let the Canadian aeronautical industry come crashing down. Of a budgeted $121.6 million for 1989-90, it will receive at best $65.6 million, and in the worst assumption $54.5 million. That, Mr. Speaker, is a 66 per cent budget cut. Imagine, 66 per cent!
Finally, when you examine those figures more thoroughly, you realize that what the Minister is proclaiming as huge investments in research and development is effectively a government exercise which will allow them in 1989 to reduce the budgets of the National Research Council and associated councils to less than the 1985-86 budget threshold. Four years from now, Mr. Speaker, we will be poorer than today as far as research is concerned. This is the progress that is being made by this Conservative Government. It's no big deal.
The Conservative Government is regressive and finds it difficult to be progressive. It is easy for them to fall back. Those figures hide a more disheartening fact, that the destruction of the research structure will jeopardize the future of our country. As I have just stated, jobs will be lost, industries as well as small- and medium-sized businesses will never see the light of day. There is another factor which I would like to point out to the House. It is the human factor. Researchers will lose their jobs. All those young people who are now getting post-secondary education and who have worked hard for years will see their career expectations in their own country dissolve into thin air. Such is the situation in Canada at this moment.
It is senseless. It is the opposite of what is being done by our trading partners who are members of the OECD. Meanwhile, in the United States, industry, as we know, is looking for more graduates, more Ph.D.s; there are more jobs available than applicants. In Canada, the opposite is true. The Conservative Government is doing away with existing jobs and is taking steps which will prevent the creation of new ones.
Mr. Speaker, I suppose the situation is rather difficult for post-graduate students in Canadian universities-they are not exactly living in the lap of luxury, and they find it very
difficult to make ends meet and find jobs. I know, because I have met several people with PhDs who are looking for jobs. Because they are unable to find them in Canada, they are planning to move abroad, and we are going to lose forever these human resources we have spent a lot of money developing; education today, I reckon, is very expensive. Mr. Speaker, we must see to it that these people have a rewarding career in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to conclude my remarks with the following comments: Students generally, at least in my riding, are not rich. They are not rolling in money. They need and seek help, and should get it. Universities have dated equipment. They need to be listened to attentively and sympathetically by the Government. They need money to update their equipment. Mr. Speaker, they need it to continue this research which is absolutely essential for the development of the healthy, progressive and modern economy which will make Canada a fine place to live in and the envy of almost every country in the world.

Mr. Speaker, I rise in the House today in my capacity of Deputy Chairman of the
Committee on Science and Technology, and I must say I totally disagree with the comments of the Hon. Member for Laurier (Mr. Berger). Nor do I agree with his motion condemning the Government for its policy on science and technology. I do not agree, because the Hon. Member has confused the issue, both for the industry, the researchers and the universities.
Personally, I can inform the Hon. Member that I have some lingering doubts and a great many questions about the goodwill of Dr. Kerwin, since last week, when he gave his press conference, he did not bother to invite the Minister or the Government Members sitting on the Standing Committee on Science and Technology. On the other hand, the Hon. Member for Laurier and the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) were both present.
Mr. Speaker, my purpose in rising in the House today is to inform the House of the performance and positive achievements of this Government since it was elected. When my colleagues and I were elected two years ago, we announced our support for a broad movement towards national reconciliation. We wanted to create a new climate for this country, a climate of consultation, co-operation and solidarity, while focussing on common goals, a climate that would put an end to confrontation and the lack of openness that for too long had cast a shadow over federal-provincial relations. Our goal was to create a true partnership between the provinces and the territories and the federal Government, a partnership whose goal would be the economic and regional development of our country, the creation of new jobs and thus the well-being of all Canadians.
This Government has achieved some significant results and the progress made in science and technology is a concrete example. Our accomplishments cannot be denied. We realize that science and technology will make it possible for us to compete on an equal footing on international markets, which, together with economic growth, will bring about job security and help maintain our standard of living. We want to use the various applications of science and technology to meet the specific needs of the regions, not just by taking advantage of existing skills and expertise but also by helping to expand the industrial bases of specific regions.
Our provincial and territorial counterparts are committed to working together with the federal Government to ensure that Canada will have a strong economic future. Since it came to power, our Government has negotiated and concluded subsidiary agreements on regional economic development with three provinces: Quebec, British Columbia and, more recently, New Brunswick. These subsidiary agreements enable the provinces and the federal Government to finance jointly certain initiatives by enhancing the development of science and technology in the provinces, and they illustrate our desire to make the applications of science and technology available to industry and to the public.
October 22, 1986

The Canada-Quebec subsidiary agreement signed on June 10, 1985 provides a $ 100-million fund over five years and features three main components. The first has to do with research centres and includes the construction of Sainte-Foy's $34 million national optics institute, in my Quebec riding, a project of which I am very proud indeed. Considered as a nonprofit corporation, the institute will be in a position to work closely with the private sector, and it will be administered by a board of directors selected from various sectors of activities and various regions of Canada. Construction will begin within a few weeks and the opening is scheduled for late 1987.
The agreement also provides for the construction of an electrochemical laboratory designed for state-of-the-art research and development in electrochemistry and electrotechnology in Shawinigan, in co-operation with Quebec Hydro, as well as funding for research projects in co-operation with the private sector. The total cost of this project is $26 million.
The second component is a technological development support program to finance feasibility studies, purchase scientific equipment, and stimulate private sector research and development initiatives.
Private business in Quebec has already reacted very enthusiastically to this $38 million program.
As a matter of fact, so far 85-odd projects have been submitted in such sectors as biotechnology, data processing, microelectronics and manufacturing processes.
Until now, about 15 projects estimated at $4 million have been funded.
The last component has to do with the coordination and integration of federal and provincial government science and technology policies and programs.
The July 8, 1985 Canada-British Columbia subsidiary agreement provides a $20 million funding over five years and meets British Columbia's priority objectives.
Under the terms of this agreement, funds are available for three projects.
The first one is aimed at strenghtening capabilities in computer science, applied mathematics, micro-electronics and robotics. In this context, we have announced recently the joint financing of the British Columbia Advanced Systems Institute, which is a first class research and education center in these areas.
The second initiative aims at promoting advances and commercial applications in the field of biotechnology. Under this program, we are financing the creation of a biotreatment centre to complement the British Columbia Biomedical Research Centre.
The purpose of the third initiative is to establish a liaison network between the industry and the universities. Under the terms of the agreement, the creation of three liaison offices has
Supply
been financed in each of the three British Columbia universities and the technological transfer results have been very encouraging to date.
As for the Canada-New Brunswick subsidiary agreement on industrial innovations and technological development signed on May 28, 1986, and involving an outlay of $28.5 million over five years, it represents a crucial stage in the industrial development of that province. This agreement is designed to support and strenghten the high technology capacity of the province, to stimulate innovation and to propose support for private businesses, individuals and manufacturer's associations with activities in technological fields or problems which could be solved by technological means.
This agreement will be implemented at a Convention on Technology in New Brunswick which will be held in Saint John on October 29 and 30, 1986.
In addition, the Federal Government has made other nonfinancial bilateral agreements with eight provinces, namely Quebec, New Brunswick, British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland.
These memoranda of agreement promote official co-operation between the Federal Government and the provinces to harmonize policies and programs and define strategies to take advantage of the opportunities available.
The Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Oberle) is convinced that bilateral agreements in science and technology are a major tool for co-operation with the provinces to stimulate regional economic development through research and development.
He therefore intends to continue his discussions with his counterparts, which will probably lead to additional subsidiary agreements in science and technology with other provinces.
I also feel compelled to mention some of our other major initiatives which illustrate the priority given to science and technology by this Government.
For the first time since 1978, the Federal and Provincial Ministers responsible for Science and Technology met in Calgary in February, 1985, to discuss matters of mutual interest.
All the Ministers stressed the important part to be played by science and technology in our economic renewal, and pledged to develop an over-all national policy on science and technology based on the economic capabilities and priorities of our provinces and territories.
Three basic priorities were identified to provide investment incentives, encourage technology transfers and applications, and support fundamental research that is important in the longer term in order to build up the scientific expertise and technical control of our country.
In September 1985, at Meech Lake, those same Ministers got further involved in preparing a national conference on

October 22, 1986
Supply
science and technology in order to make sure that everyone involved, that is, Governments, universities, unions, the industry and related organizations be given an opportunity to discuss the urgent problems to be addressed by Canada.
The first national Conference on science and technology which was held in Winnipeg last June turned out to be a consultation exercise that brought us closer to our objective, that is to achieve a national consensus on science and technology policies. The conference emphasized the need for supervision and leadership from all government levels in science and technology. That meeting brought to the fore the need to develop a national policy that would allow Canada to remain competitive from an economic viewpoint and our industries to have a capability to break new ground in areas where science and technology are essential to Canada's economic strength.
The throne speech also brought to light the federal government's interest in playing a leading and counselling role in science and technology.
Mr. Speaker, the federal government, with full co-operation of the provinces, will aim at enhancing the level of excellence and expertise in technical training, development and innovations.
On the basis of discussions held at the national Conference and national policy developments between the provinces and the federal government, the latter intends to organize a national conference on technological innovations to help setting new goals for Canadian technology in the context of a federal strategy and a rational policy.
Several of our trading partners have undertaken concerted and coordinated efforts with a view to revitalizing existing industries and creating new high tech companies. We are actively pursuing this goal through national strategies and programs involving the technological, scientific and industrial infrastructures of those countries.
Canada cannot afford to take a back seat and be satisfied with an 11th, 12th, or 13th position. Canada needs to take the lead. Scientific and technological infrastructures must be better coordinated, more efficient, more up to date, and better adapted to the social consequences of technology. Therefore, we must enhance Canada's capabilities, Mr. Speaker, while focusing on regional disparities to make sure that all regions will benefit from this new challenge.

Member for Laurier (Mr. Berger), Mr. Speaker, I want to tell him first of all that we do not administer this country on the basis of the stupidities one can read in the papers. October 22, 1986

There is something I should like to tell Canadians concerning the famous five-year plan this Government granted to the National Research Council, something the previous Liberal Government had failed to do, because it preferred to pay out small ad hoc amounts now and then, not always regularly. This infamous deficit which we have inherited from our predecessors and compels us to make cuts in all Government Departments and Agencies. Well, we have had enough of that. Bravo, Suzanne!

Member for Louis-Hebert can quote a statement from the National Research Council, but I ask her once more, as elected representative of Quebec City, to apologize to the former Dean of Laval University, Mr. Larkin Kerwin, a distinguished scholar born in Quebec City who is now head of the National Research Council of Canada. Mr. Speaker, I attach quite heavy significance to the debate this afternoon. While it is inevitable in this political Chamber that the debate be political, I thought we might have heard debate of a slightly higher level, both in terms of reasonableness and logic and of the temper of that debate. Instead, we heard an outburst of sound and fury moments ago which signified nothing. We heard the claim that for many people reallocation has not meant the loss of jobs. speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext: That's nonsense.
That's an exaggeration.
Let us not kid ourselves. The absurdity of this debate is manifested by members of the Party in power.
What about your own distortion?

Every Member knows that I am not saying that the United States is a superior country. I am saying that Canada has the necessary creativity and resources and ought to have the guts, foresight and intelligence to use that creativity in a way which will benefit our citizens, in terms of both economic pay-off and the ability to pay for our programs of social justice and the security of equality for the people of our country.
That is exactly what we are doing.

As the Hon. Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Oberle) knows, the problem in this country is that we have until now been a resource-based nation. We have been fairly successful in that. By virtue of our exports we have been able to sustain a level of social justice which is unchallenged by most countries in the world. I think members of most political Parties would support that. The fact is that those resources are falling in price and are subject to increased competition from around the world and to substitution. They are, therefore, endangered.
We are faced with competition in a knowledge-based world. In such a world Canada will not be able to compete unless it does something about its ability to produce as a result of and on the basis of what we know. If our resources are to profit us they will do so only on the basis of an absolute national commitment to use research, science and technology to convert

our resources to products available to nations around the world. We need a science and technology policy not directed to the enhancement of defence-linked expenditures, but rather to expenditures which will produce products demanded by a peaceful world.
We quite evidently have a need to take some bold initiatives to ensure the economic survival of this country. speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext: What a crock.

As the Science Council pointed out, we are talking about competing, on a free trade basis, with a nation which spends huge amounts of money. The federal Government of that country spends 77 per cent of its research funds on defence. Comparable government expenditures in Canada run around 9 per cent. To open ourselves up without considerable preparation is going to put a great deal of our scientific and research community at risk. Indeed, it could be fairly argued that we should not even be talking about it until we have addressed the need.
There has been a great deal of comparison this afternoon between what the Liberals have done and what the Conservatives have done on science and research. We have heard vague allegations that those of us committed to social justice are somehow opposed to reasonable choices and decisions with respect to science. Let us be perfectly clear that we are in a sorry state. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) recognized this in the book he wrote before becoming Prime Minister. To paraphrase, he said that we are in danger of becoming a Junior B team in the league of science. Of course, that is true. One point three per cent of the GNP is devoted to research, compared to 2.5 per cent in all the other leading industrial nations of the world. Among OECD countries we rank about tenth.
The Minister of State for Science and Technology has said, in justifying some of the changes with respect to government and scientific establishments, that our Government spends disproportionately on science as compared to industry. The fact is that we rank tenth among OECD countries in the amount of government expenditures on science. In the industrial sector we rank thirteenth. If we look at any of the other criteria for scientific and technological performance, we are in trouble. A $20 billion deficit in technological exports has already been cited. There was reason for the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) to say that we had better get on the starting line for the technological revolution.
We have heard members of the Liberal Party criticize this present Government. The Liberals have produced a sorry record regarding their policies with respect to science and technology. That is undoubtedly clear. It has already been pointed out that they failed to commit themselves to proper five-year funding plans for the granting agencies. Indeed, they interrupted the five-year plan that the Clark Government introduced in 1979. We all know about the scientific tax credit boondoggle. It is difficult to argue that any of the politicians in power in the last hundred years have had the commitment to research, science and technology that is appropriate to our future economic development. There is no doubt that the Liberals were bad.
When the Prime Minister said that we must become "major league" in the scientific enterprise, we had much to hope for. Some recent initiatives have been helpful. Some focus has been brought to bear on the issue of research, science and technology-
Hear, hear!

I would submit that there has been more public discussion and debate about the issue in recent weeks than there has been in my memory. There have been some initiatives that in context have to be praised. The creation of a National Advisory Board with the Prime Minister as chairman has the potential to be a significant initiative.
Hear, hear!

The promise of a national science and technology strategy is helpful in that it has been repeated, although it is slow in coming. But promises made in other forums, vague promises of more co-operative talking together, the other two parts of that four part program, are not helpful at all. At least there has been a salutary focus. The exaggerated rhetoric and the dangerous misleading of the public about what is being done is not helpful.
We have been told that there will be $800 million in new money for space-based research. That is not new money. There has been no net addition. We are having a debate now about reallocation from NRC in order to fund that. Why not at least be truthful? Why not present the facts to permit a reasonable informed analysis of what the Government is doing?
I would like to read the so-called contradiction identified by the Minister of State for Science and Technology in the question I asked him, which was: Who among the scientific community suggested that the NRC be savaged to support a space program. With respect to the space program, Howard McCurdy said on March 27, 1985 that I do support and would support scientifically and politically the involvement of Canada in a space station used for peaceful purposes. But not by savaging the NRC. Remember Pinocchio, Mr. Speaker. Early in the spring, we were all shocked, including the Minister, about the announcement that RRAP was to be cut by some $60 million. It has not been cut. There has been some scurrying around and instead we are going to have some

reallocation within NRC. This reallocation is going to put people out of jobs. There is a certain accuracy but a certain lack of precision in the message being communicated about what this Government is doing. We are told that $1 billion is going into university research.
Hear, hear!

The implication is that this is new money. If you look at the Minister's own figures, at the very best, $730 million of additional money will go into university research, if the industrial community contributes to the three granting councils 500 per cent more than it ever has in the last few years. Still there is a considerable gap of more than $250 million in what the Minister says he is going to do and what is actually being done. We have to remind ourselves of Pinocchio. In measuring the value of that exaggerated increase, we must remember that $738 million is exactly half of what NSERC alone indicated was required to meet the need-never mind MRC, never mind SSHRC. We were misled. What that will mean is that there will be under the most optimistic predictions a 2.9 per cent real increase in the amount of money going to the granting agencies.
What we need is honesty. We do need a rational science, research and technology policy. We do not expect the changes to occur overnight. We do not expect them to occur by virtue of the irrational attack on programs already existing to feed pie-in-the-sky notions of what is politically convenient.
There are some suggestions that could be made. The very essence of all of this is that one of the problems that this nation
Supply
has must be addressed, that is, its orientation towards a resource based versus a knowledge-based society. That suggests that there should be some serious initiatives taken by the Government in the reform of university and secondary education generally in terms of our arrangements for funding the universities. In this commitment to science and technology, $2 billion has been cut from the expected increases in funding at the university level over the next five years. That is another action this Government has taken that could not possibly be consistent with a rational science and technology policy. There need to be some reforms in post-secondary, secondary, and primary eduction commensurate with our new thrust in science and technology. That should include more technical training. We have to recognize the basic importance of science, research and technology by placing the Minister of State for Science and Technology in the Priorities and Planning Committee of the Cabinet where he belongs. If you refer to the CAUTNT bulletin you will find some other useful suggestions that would serve to advise this Government on a policy it is struggling to achieve and which is necessary for this country.
